analysis.one_liner: Lets either party to a manufacturer-dealer sales and service contract opt out of forced arbitration.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the House Judiciary Committee; it got a hearing but no vote before the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When a manufacturer sells a product to a dealer who also repairs and services it, and the contract requires arbitration of disputes, this bill would have let either side decline arbitration once a dispute actually arises. It also would have required arbitrators to give written reasons for their awards and let courts throw out awards that misread state law. The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee, sent to a subcommittee, received a hearing, and died there without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Franchise dealers — most notably auto and equipment dealerships — who are typically the smaller, weaker party in manufacturer contracts. After a dispute arises, they could refuse arbitration and take the manufacturer to court instead, where rules of evidence and appeal apply. The written-reason requirement and the ability of courts to vacate awards that misapply state law would also have made any arbitration that did happen more reviewable and transparent.

how_it_helps.text: Each party to a sales and service contract with an arbitration clause — defined as a contract where a manufacturer sells a product for resale and authorizes repair and service — may reject arbitration in writing after a dispute arises and before arbitration begins.
Arbitrators must give the parties a written explanation of the reasons for the award, making decisions harder to issue without justification.
A court may vacate an award if the arbitrator disregarded, misapplied, or misinterpreted state law, giving courts real power to correct awards instead of near-automatic deference.
The changes apply to contracts entered into, amended, renewed, or extended after enactment, so manufacturers could not simply leave old arbitration clauses in place through routine renewals.

analysis.who_pays: Manufacturers, importers, and distributors that used mandatory arbitration clauses in their dealer contracts would lose their ability to keep disputes out of court, and would face greater litigation costs and court oversight. The arbitration industry would see fewer cases and less finality in its awards.

drawbacks.text: Arbitration is usually faster and cheaper than a courtroom. Allowing either party to reject arbitration after a dispute arises could push both sides into costlier, slower litigation even when arbitration would have worked fine for them.

Letting a court vacate any award that 'disregarded, misapplied, or misinterpreted' state law would loosen the finality that makes arbitration attractive, inviting losers in arbitration to relitigate their cases in court.

The bill does not touch consumer contracts directly; its protections apply to manufacturer-to-dealer sales, so shoppers with arbitration clauses in their own purchase contracts would not gain an opt-out under this text.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's core benefit — a one-sided 'take it or leave it' arbitration clause can no longer be forced on the party with less power — is real, and the written-reason and judicial-review requirements would have improved accountability. The costs are higher dispute expenses and less finality, but because either party can reject arbitration and can still choose it, the bill preserves arbitration as an option rather than abolishing it. On balance it modestly rebalances power between large manufacturers and the dealers they deal with.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Judiciary Committee, then to a subcommittee that held a hearing, and it never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on July 31, 1991, with ten original sponsors from both parties, and referred to the House Committee on Judiciary.
In April 1992 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law, which held hearings in June 1992.
No further action was taken; the committee never marked up or reported the bill, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, without a vote in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Manufacturers that impose mandatory arbitration clauses on their dealers kept the status quo, since the bill never became law. Dealers remained bound by the arbitration provisions in their contracts.

for.name: Rep. John W. Bryant
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let parties to manufacturer-dealer contracts reject arbitration and to require reasoned, reviewable awards.

for.name: 25 cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it bipartisan support.

for.name: Subcommittee on Economic and Commercial Law
for.what_they_did: Held hearings on the bill in June 1992.

against.name: House Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral under Chair Jack Brooks
against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to a subcommittee and never scheduled a markup or reported it out, leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had bipartisan sponsorship — 14 Democrats, 10 Republicans, and 1 Independent among 25 cosponsors — but no roll-call votes were ever taken, so the party split on the substance was never tested.

industries.note: The bill would have ended their ability to force dealer disputes into arbitration on the manufacturer's terms, exposing them to court suits and judicial review. Their interest in keeping disputes out of court ran against the smaller dealers and, indirectly, the transparency consumers rely on.

Dealers, usually the smaller party, could have opted for court after a dispute arose instead of facing a manufacturer-chosen arbitration process. Dealer fortunes in disputes are closely tied to fair treatment of the local businesses consumers deal with.
Fewer mandatory cases and written-reason and vacatur requirements would have reduced demand for arbitration and its insulation from courts.
